title: Euler's Formula from the Taylor Series as Definitions
description: Reverses the foundational dependency of the parent entry. Rather than defining cos/sin via the exponential and deriving their power series, here cosSeries and sinSeries are *defined* by their Maclaurin series, and Euler's formula e^{iz} = cosSeries z + i·sinSeries z is proved directly from the exponential series e^w = Σ wⁿ/n!: regrouping the sum over ℕ into even-indexed (n=2k) and odd-indexed (n=2k+1) parts splits e^{iz} into exactly the cosine and sine series. The core derivation (hasSum_euler, euler_formula) makes no appeal to the value of Complex.cos; Mathlib's cosine is invoked only at the end to identify the series-definitions with the standard functions and to recover Euler's identity e^{iπ} = −1. Verified, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

relatedProblems.relationship: Parent: derives the Taylor series of cos/sin from the exponential definition. This entry answers its first open question — the reverse dependency: take the Taylor series as definitions and prove Euler's formula.

overview.historicalContext: Euler's formula e^{ix} = cos x + i·sin x can be founded in two opposite ways. Mathlib's choice defines cos/sin through the exponential, cos z = (e^{iz}+e^{−iz})/2, and proves the power series as theorems (the parent entry, euler-identity-oq-01-oq-02). The classical alternative, going back to Euler's Introductio (1748), takes the Maclaurin series cos z = Σ (−1)ⁿ z²ⁿ/(2n)! and sin z = Σ (−1)ⁿ z²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n+1)! as the *definitions* of the trigonometric functions and derives Euler's formula by splitting the exponential series e^{iz} = Σ (iz)ⁿ/n! into its even and odd parts. This entry formalizes that reverse direction, the parent's explicitly stated first open question.
overview.problemStatement: Define cos and sin by their Maclaurin series and prove Euler's exponential formula e^{iz} = cos z + i·sin z directly from the exponential series, without going through Mathlib's exponential definition of cos. Recover the Pythagorean identity and Euler's identity e^{iπ} = −1 within this framework.
overview.proofStrategy: Start from the single fact e^{iz} = Σ (iz)ⁿ/n! (expSeries_div_hasSum_exp). Transport this HasSum across the equivalence ℕ ≃ ℕ × Fin 2 (Nat.divModEquiv 2) and collapse fibers with HasSum.prod_fiberwise: the k-th fiber sum is (iz)^{2k}/(2k)! + (iz)^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!, which simplifies — via I² = −1 — to cosTerm k + i·sinTerm k. This gives hasSum_euler. The cosine and sine series are separately shown summable by comparing their norms with the exponential series of ‖z‖ (Summable.of_norm_bounded together with Summable.comp_injective along k ↦ 2k and k ↦ 2k+1). Combining the two convergent series with hasSum_euler and the uniqueness of sums yields euler_formula. Only afterwards are the series identified with Complex.cos/sin (cos_eq_tsum/sin_eq_tsum) to deduce Pythagoras and Euler's identity.
keyInsights: The entire reversal rests on one resummation: the exponential series over ℕ regroups, via n = 2k and n = 2k+1, into the even part (cosine) and the odd part (i times sine). This is the same equivalence Mathlib uses to prove cos_eq_tsum, run in the opposite logical direction.

I² = −1 is exactly what turns the even powers (iz)^{2k} = (−1)ᵏ z^{2k} into the cosine series and the odd powers (iz)^{2k+1} = (−1)ᵏ i z^{2k+1} into i times the sine series; after rewriting I^{2k} = (−1)ᵏ the fiber identity is closed by ring.

Convergence of the cosine/sine series needs no trigonometric input: each is a subseries of the absolutely convergent exponential series for ‖z‖, reached by composing with the injective reindexings k ↦ 2k and k ↦ 2k+1.
Because the value of e^{iz} is pinned by the series alone, the equality e^{iz} = cosSeries z + i·sinSeries z follows from uniqueness of sums — no property of Complex.cos is used in the derivation.

Once Euler's formula holds for the series-definitions, every classical consequence (Pythagoras cos²+sin²=1, Euler's identity e^{iπ}=−1) is recovered by identifying the series with Mathlib's cos/sin, closing the loop with the parent entry.

sections.title: Header: Euler's Formula from the Taylor Series as Definitions
sections.summary: States the open question — reverse the parent chain's foundational dependency by taking the Maclaurin series for sin and cos as the definitions of the trigonometric functions, then proving Euler's exponential formula e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x from them. This file defines cosSeries/sinSeries by their series and derives Euler's formula directly from the exponential series e^w = Σ wⁿ/n! by regrouping the sum over ℕ into even- and odd-indexed parts (via Nat.divModEquiv 2 and HasSum.prod_fiberwise), splitting e^{iz} into cosSeries z + i·sinSeries z without ever appealing to the value of Complex.cos in the core derivation; Mathlib's cosine is invoked only at the end to identify the series-definitions with the standard functions and recover e^{iπ} = −1. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
sections.mathContext: $e^{iz} = \sum_n (iz)^n/n! = \sum_k (iz)^{2k}/(2k)! + \sum_k (iz)^{2k+1}/(2k+1)! = \mathrm{cosSeries}(z) + i\,\mathrm{sinSeries}(z)$, by even/odd regrouping of the exponential series.

sections.title: Section III: Euler's Formula by Even/Odd Resummation

sections.mathContext: The heart of the reversed dependency: Euler's formula derived from the exponential series alone.

sections.title: Section IV: Identification and Euler's Identity
sections.summary: cosSeries_eq_cos / sinSeries_eq_sin identify the series with Complex.cos/sin; pythagoras gives cos²+sin²=1; euler_formula_real records the real form; euler_identity recovers e^{iπ} = −1.
sections.mathContext: Closing the loop with the parent entry and the standard trigonometric functions.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 128 lines, 2 definitions and 9 theorems, formalizing the reverse foundational route to Euler's formula. cos and sin are defined by their Maclaurin series; their convergence is proved by comparison with the exponential series; and Euler's formula e^{iz} = cosSeries z + i·sinSeries z is derived directly from e^{iz} = Σ (iz)ⁿ/n! by regrouping into even and odd parts, with no appeal to the value of Complex.cos. The Pythagorean identity and Euler's identity e^{iπ} = −1 are then recovered by identifying the series with Mathlib's trigonometric functions.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent entry's first open question. Where the parent runs Mathlib's dependency (cos defined via exp ⟹ power series), this entry runs the classical one (series as definition ⟹ Euler's formula), and the two meet at cosSeries_eq_cos/sinSeries_eq_sin. The core lemma hasSum_euler isolates the genuine mathematical content — the even/odd resummation of the exponential series — making explicit that Euler's formula is exactly the statement that e^{iz} decomposes into its even and odd parts.
openQuestions: Develop the trigonometric addition formulas cos(z+w), sin(z+w) directly from the series-definitions (via the Cauchy product of the cosine and sine series) rather than from the exponential, completing a self-contained series-first development.

Use the series-defined cos/sin to prove the derivative relations cos' = −sin and sin' = cos by differentiating the power series term by term, recovering the analytic characterization from the definitional one.
